cards.title: Who ruled Bengal before the Company?
cards.idea: In the 1750s, Bengal was ruled by the Nawab, a powerful Muslim ruler who controlled trade, taxes, and the army. The East India Company was just one merchant among many.

interaction.prompt: Tap to see who held real power in Bengal

cards.reveal: The Nawab of Bengal held absolute power. The Company had a small trading post at Calcutta but no political control.

cards.title: The Battle of Plassey, 1757
cards.idea: Robert Clive led the Company's army against the Nawab's much larger force. Clive secretly bribed the Nawab's general Mir Jafar to betray him, turning the battle without a real fight.

interaction.prompt: Tap to reveal what happened during the battle

cards.reveal: Mir Jafar switched sides mid-battle. The Nawab's army collapsed. Clive won with fewer than 1,000 soldiers against 50,000. The Company now controlled Bengal's government.

cards.title: From trader to ruler
cards.idea: After Plassey, the Company installed Mir Jafar as a puppet Nawab who obeyed Company orders. The Company now collected taxes, commanded the army, and made laws in Bengal.

interaction.prompt: Tap to see what the Company now controlled

cards.reveal: The Company transformed from a business into a government. It taxed farmers, controlled courts, and built a private army. Bengal became the Company's first major territory in India.

cards.title: Why did the Nawab lose?
cards.idea: The Nawab trusted his generals and did not expect betrayal. He also underestimated the Company's military discipline and European weapons like cannons.

interaction.prompt: Tap to understand the Nawab's mistake

cards.reveal: The Nawab had numbers but not unity. Mir Jafar's betrayal broke his army's will to fight. The Company's smaller, disciplined force and superior tactics won the day.

cards.title: The ripple effect
cards.idea: Bengal's wealth—its taxes, trade, and resources—now flowed to the Company. This money funded the Company's expansion into other Indian regions and strengthened British power.

interaction.prompt: Tap to see the long-term impact

cards.reveal: Bengal became the base for Company rule across India. The wealth extracted from Bengal paid for armies that conquered Madras, Bombay, and eventually most of India by 1850.

cards.title: A turning point
cards.idea: Before Plassey, the Company was one merchant among many. After Plassey, it became a territorial power. This shift from trade to conquest changed India's history forever.

interaction.prompt: Tap to see why Plassey mattered

cards.reveal: Plassey proved the Company could defeat Indian rulers militarily and politically. It showed that betrayal, bribery, and discipline could overcome larger armies. Other Indian rulers did not see this threat until it was too late.

workbook.prompt: Who was bribed by Robert Clive to betray the Nawab at the Battle of Plassey?
After winning at Plassey in 1757, the East India Company transformed from a trading business into a ________ in Bengal.
What was the main reason the Nawab's large army lost to Clive's smaller force?
options: The Nawab's general betrayed him and switched sides
The Nawab's soldiers were untrained and had no weapons
The British had superior numbers and better horses
The Nawab refused to fight and surrendered immediately
workbook.answer: The Nawab's general betrayed him and switched sides

boss.prompt: How did the Company's control of Bengal enable its expansion into other parts of India?
options: Bengal's taxes and resources funded armies that conquered other regions
The Nawab of Bengal agreed to help the Company attack neighboring kingdoms
Bengal's location on the coast made it easy to import soldiers from Britain
Other Indian rulers voluntarily joined the Company after hearing about Plassey
boss.answer: Bengal's taxes and resources funded armies that conquered other regions

boss.prompt: The Battle of ________ in 1757 marked the moment when the East India Company shifted from being a merchant to being a territorial ruler in India.
Why did other Indian rulers not immediately recognize the threat posed by the Company after Plassey?
options: They believed the Company's victory was a one-time lucky event and did not understand its military and political strategy
They were too busy fighting each other and did not pay attention to events in Bengal
The Company kept its victory secret and did not tell other rulers what had happened
Indian rulers had already defeated European armies before and were not afraid of the Company
boss.answer: They believed the Company's victory was a one-time lucky event and did not understand its military and political strategy
